resources.string: This credential may not change it: it needs the %1$s scope.

Who may reach what in the tailnet, with SSH rules, tags and tests, exactly as the server keeps it, comments included. A change is checked here and by the server, compared with this version and sent only if nobody changed the file meanwhile.
Saved on this phone before its last change to the policy (%1$s). Reverting goes through every check a change does.
The tailnet\'s settings say the policy comes from elsewhere, such as GitOps or Terraform: edits here would be overwritten, so it is read-only. Change it where it is managed.
This credential may read the policy file but not change it: that needs the policy_file scope.
Reads as a policy file. The server checks it again on review.
Nothing has been sent; the policy stays as it is.
Line %1$d: a string is not closed.
Line %1$d: a /* comment is not closed.
The %1$s opened on line %2$d is never closed.
Line %1$d: %2$s does not close what line %3$d opened.
Line %1$d: the file ends too early.
Line %1$d: a colon is missing after the key.
Line %1$d: a comma is missing before this.
The policy must be one object in braces.
Next you type «%1$s» and unlock; then it is sent only if the file is still the version you started from.
Checked by the server, tests included
The file does not read as a policy
The server could not check it
Nothing this check knows to be risky is new.
The text is the same as the current version: nothing to send.
This phone keeps the access it had, as far as the previews show.
As %1$s this phone no longer reaches: %2$s
No longer allowed to reach this phone at %1$s: %2$s
This phone is not a node of this tailnet, so its own access was not checked.
The access check could not run: %1$s

The server previews which rules match this phone\'s user and its address on ports 22 and 443, under the current policy and under the new one. A rule rewritten to say the same thing differently shows up here too.
“*” as a source lets every user and device of the tailnet use this rule.
“*” as a destination reaches every device in the tailnet on these ports.
Everyone, including users and devices shared in from other tailnets.
An SSH rule with “*” among its sources, destinations or users opens shells far wider than one host or group.
SSH as root without a check
“accept” lets these users log in as root with no re-authentication; “check” would ask for it.
Routes or exit nodes announced by anyone in this group are approved with no admin looking at them.
A route of /8 or wider (IPv6 /32), up to the whole internet, is approved automatically.
Funnel publishes services to the public internet; this lets every member or device turn it on.
Tests are what the server checks every policy change against; removing them removes that guard.
Every device follows the new rules within seconds. The version it replaces stays on this phone for a revert.
The server refused it when it checked it again: %1$s
Changed elsewhere, and the new version could not be read: %1$s
The policy file was changed after you opened it, and your edit was not sent. Nothing of theirs or yours is lost yet.
Your edit and theirs touch different lines: yours can be applied on top of theirs and reviewed again.
Your edit and theirs touch the same place, around lines %1$s.
Apply my edit to their version
The server shows which rules of the saved policy let traffic through: to a device on a port, or from a user. Nothing is changed.
No rule lets anyone reach it on this port.
No rule lets this user reach anything.
Every device gets a name in the tailnet, like host.tailnet.ts.net, that the others resolve.
There is no global nameserver: the server may refuse MagicDNS without one.
Names like host.tailnet.ts.net stop resolving on every device; devices reach each other by address only, and anything set up by name breaks.
Devices use the global nameservers below for every name, instead of the DNS their own network gives them.
Add a global nameserver first: with none, devices would have no resolver.
This server has only the older DNS API, which cannot set it.
Every device resolves every name through the global nameservers, ignoring its own network\'s DNS.
Devices go back to their own network\'s DNS for names outside the tailnet.
Resolvers for names outside the tailnet: an IPv4 or IPv6 address, or a DNS-over-HTTPS URL. “Exit node” keeps a resolver in use while a device goes through an exit node.
Use these also with an exit node
The last global nameserver goes, and the server turns MagicDNS off with it: names like host.tailnet.ts.net stop resolving until MagicDNS is turned on again.
Override local DNS is on: with no global nameserver, devices are left without a resolver for names outside the tailnet.
Names under a domain go to its own resolvers, such as an office DNS reached through a subnet router.
Short names are tried under these domains: “wiki” becomes wiki.example.com.
An IPv4 or IPv6 address, or an https:// DoH URL.
A DNS-over-HTTPS URL starts with https:// and has a host.
A domain: letters, digits and hyphens, in labels separated by dots.
Tailscale posts events to these addresses as they happen: a new device to approve, a key about to expire. A phone cannot receive them; they are for a chat or a server.
Queued at once; the endpoint receives an event of type “test” within seconds.
A new signing secret, shown once. The old one stops working at once.
https, on port 443 or 80, reachable from the internet.
Not an address Tailscale can post to.
The address must start with https://.
Tailscale posts only to port 443 or 80.
No user name or password in the address: the secret signs each event instead.
Events go to %1$s from now on. Its signing secret is shown once, next.
Only the chosen events are posted to this endpoint.
A new signing secret is made and shown once; the old one stops working.
Until the endpoint has the new secret, it rejects every event as forged.
A device key expires within a day
A subnet router has IP forwarding off
An exit node has IP forwarding off
This credential cannot read it (it needs %1$s).
Regional routing: %1$s. It follows the route selection.
New devices wait for an admin\'s approval before they can connect.
New users wait for an admin\'s approval before they can join.
How long a device stays logged in before it must re-authenticate; from 1 to 180 days.
Which of your users may join other tailnets they are invited to.
Tailscale updates itself on the devices that support it.
Devices may get TLS certificates for their tailnet names, which Serve and Funnel use. Every such name is published in public Certificate Transparency logs.
How a route served by several subnet routers picks one.
Tailscale logs every connection between devices: who, to whom, when, how much.
Devices report identifiers such as serial numbers to device-posture integrations.
Marks the policy as managed elsewhere (GitOps, Terraform): the console stops editing it, and so does this app.
A link the console shows to where the policy really lives; https, or empty.
An https:// link with a host, or nothing.
New devices join without an admin approving them: anyone who can log in, or holds an auth key, adds a device at once.
New devices wait for an admin\'s approval; devices already in stay.
New users join without an admin approving them.
New users wait for an admin\'s approval; users already in stay.
Devices stay logged in longer before they must re-authenticate: a lost or stolen device keeps its access longer.
Devices re-authenticate sooner, from their next login on.
More of your users may join other tailnets, taking their devices there.
Fewer of your users may join other tailnets.
Tailscale updates itself on every device that supports it.
Devices update only when their owners update them.
Devices may get certificates, and every name that gets one is published in public Certificate Transparency logs, for good.
No new certificates: Serve and Funnel over HTTPS stop working as the current ones expire.
Every device picks among subnet routers serving the same routes the new way.
Every connection in the tailnet is logged and kept by Tailscale: who talked to whom, when and how much.
Connections are no longer logged; logs already kept age out on their own.
Devices start reporting identifiers such as serial numbers to posture integrations.
Devices stop reporting identity; posture rules that rely on it may stop matching.
The policy can no longer be edited in the console or here; it is expected to come from your external pipeline.
The policy can be edited in the console again; an external pipeline may overwrite those edits.
The console links to this address as where the policy is managed.
